mcqs.q: The functional unit of the kidney is the:
mcqs.explain: Each kidney has about a million nephrons; a nephron is a renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule) plus renal tubules.

mcqs.q: Which is an ENDOCRINE function of the kidney?
opts: Secretion of erythropoietin and activation of vitamin D
mcqs.explain: The kidney secretes erythropoietin and renin and activates vitamin D, besides excreting waste and balancing fluids/electrolytes/pH.

mcqs.q: Acute kidney injury is defined as an abrupt loss of renal function over:
mcqs.explain: AKI is an abrupt deterioration over 48–72 hours with retention of nitrogenous waste; it is a medical emergency but usually reversible.

mcqs.q: A POST-renal cause of acute kidney injury is:
opts: Urinary tract obstruction (e.g. renal stone or prostatic hypertrophy)
mcqs.explain: Post-renal AKI is due to urinary tract obstruction (stone, stricture, prostatic hypertrophy); pre-renal = reduced blood flow; renal = parenchymal/vessel disorders.

mcqs.q: Chronic kidney disease is defined as a deterioration of renal function lasting:
opts: More than 3 months, progressive and irreversible (GFR <60)
mcqs.explain: CKD is a longstanding (>3 months), progressive and irreversible decline, with a high creatinine and GFR <60 mL/min.

mcqs.q: The most common cause of end-stage renal disease is:
mcqs.explain: Diabetes (≈42%) and hypertension (≈28%) are the leading causes of ESRD, followed by glomerular and congenital disease.

mcqs.q: Anaemia in chronic kidney disease is mainly due to:
mcqs.explain: The failing kidney makes less erythropoietin (plus marrow depression and blood loss), causing a normocytic normochromic anaemia.

mcqs.q: Renal osteodystrophy develops because phosphate retention leads to:
opts: Low calcium and secondary hyperparathyroidism, with low active vitamin D
High calcium and low parathyroid hormone
mcqs.explain: Phosphate retention lowers plasma calcium, raising PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism); the kidney also fails to activate vitamin D, weakening bone.

mcqs.q: Which oral sign reflects the systemic effects of CKD?
opts: Xerostomia with a metallic taste and mucosal pallor
mcqs.explain: CKD causes xerostomia (→ candidiasis, halitosis, metallic taste, caries), uraemic stomatitis and mucosal pallor from anaemia.

mcqs.q: Gingival overgrowth in a transplant patient is most often caused by:
mcqs.explain: Gingival overgrowth is a side effect of cyclosporine and nifedipine; cyclosporine is widely used for immunosuppression after transplant.

mcqs.q: A radiographic feature of renal osteodystrophy in the jaws is:
opts: Loss of the lamina dura with osteolytic radiolucencies
mcqs.explain: Disturbed calcium/phosphate metabolism causes loss of the lamina dura, osteoporosis and osteolytic radiolucent jaw lesions, with loosening of teeth.

mcqs.q: Typical biochemistry in CKD shows:
opts: High potassium and phosphate with low calcium and bicarbonate
mcqs.explain: CKD shows high urea/creatinine, high K⁺ and phosphate, low Na⁺/Ca²⁺/HCO₃, and a metabolic acidosis on ABG.

mcqs.q: Which renal replacement option is generally MORE effective than chronic dialysis?
mcqs.explain: Transplantation enhances quality of life and is more effective than chronic dialysis, ideally from a living relative before dialysis is needed.

mcqs.q: All renal transplant recipients require:
opts: A second kidney within a year
mcqs.explain: Recipients need lifelong immunosuppression to prevent rejection, which raises the risk of infection, malignancy, new-onset diabetes and hypertension.

mcqs.q: Before a planned renal transplant, the dental priority is to:
opts: Screen for and treat all dental infection
mcqs.explain: Patients are screened and treated for all infections, including dental, before transplant to prevent post-transplant complications under immunosuppression.

mcqs.q: When should routine dental treatment of a haemodialysis patient ideally be performed?
mcqs.explain: Avoid treatment on the dialysis day (heparin-related bleeding); it is best carried out the day after dialysis.

mcqs.q: When treating a dialysis patient with an arteriovenous fistula, you must:
opts: Never take BP, cannulate or inject in the fistula arm
Use the fistula arm for the BP cuff
Place an IV cannula in the fistula
mcqs.explain: Never use the fistula/shunt arm for BP, cannulation or injection — risk of fistula infection or thrombophlebitis.

mcqs.q: Which analgesic group should be AVOIDED in renal failure?
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs/aspirin are nephrotoxic and cause GI bleeding, peripheral oedema and worsening heart failure; paracetamol is preferred.

mcqs.q: Which antibiotic is best AVOIDED in renal failure because it worsens nitrogen retention and acidosis?
mcqs.explain: Tetracycline worsens nitrogen retention and acidosis and is avoided; doxycycline or minocycline may be used instead.

mcqs.q: Regarding fluoride in a CKD patient:
opts: Systemic fluoride should be avoided, but topical fluoride is safe
mcqs.explain: Damaged kidneys excrete fluoride poorly, so systemic fluoride is avoided; topical fluoride can be used safely for caries prophylaxis.

mcqs.q: Local anaesthesia in a renal failure patient is:
opts: Safe unless there is a severe bleeding tendency
mcqs.explain: LA is safe unless there is a severe bleeding tendency; conscious sedation with midazolam is preferred for sedation.

mcqs.q: A dangerous complication of major surgery in renal failure is:
opts: Hyperkalaemia causing arrhythmias or cardiac arrest
mcqs.explain: Tissue damage, acidosis and transfusion can raise potassium; hyperkalaemia predisposes to arrhythmias and may cause cardiac arrest.

mcqs.q: General anaesthesia is contraindicated in renal failure when the haemoglobin is:
opts: Any level — GA is always fine
mcqs.explain: GA (a myocardial depressant causing hypotension) is contraindicated if Hb is below 10 g/dL; isoflurane/sevoflurane are safer agents.

mcqs.q: Which antibiotic is CONTRAINDICATED in a transplant patient taking cyclosporine?
mcqs.explain: Erythromycin is contraindicated with cyclosporine (it raises cyclosporine levels/nephrotoxicity).

mcqs.q: For haemostasis during dental surgery in a renal patient, a useful agent is:
opts: Desmopressin (DDAVP), giving haemostasis for up to ~4 hours
mcqs.explain: Desmopressin can provide haemostasis for up to 4 hours; if it fails, cryoprecipitate (peak 4–12 h, lasting up to 36 h) can be used.

mcqs.q: Uraemic stomatitis and oral mucosal pallor in a renal patient reflect:
opts: Uraemia and the anaemia of CKD
mcqs.explain: Uraemic stomatitis arises from high urea, and mucosal pallor reflects the anaemia of chronic kidney disease.

mcqs.q: Before invasive dental treatment in CKD, appropriate screening includes:
opts: CBC and bleeding time, with blood-pressure monitoring
mcqs.explain: Screen with CBC and bleeding time and monitor blood pressure (avoiding the shunt arm); avoid treatment if the disease is unstable.

saqs.q: List the functions of the kidney.
saqs.a: Excretion of waste; regulation of fluid, electrolytes and pH; endocrine functions — renin, vitamin-D activation and erythropoietin secretion.

saqs.q: Contrast AKI and CKD, and give the leading causes of ESRD.
saqs.a: AKI: abrupt (48–72 h), usually reversible. CKD: >3 months, progressive, irreversible, GFR <60. Leading ESRD causes: diabetes (42%) and hypertension (28%).

saqs.q: Explain the anaemia and bone disease of CKD.
saqs.a: Anaemia: erythropoietin deficiency (+ marrow depression, blood loss). Renal osteodystrophy: phosphate retention → low calcium → secondary hyperparathyroidism + low active vitamin D.

saqs.q: List the oral manifestations of CKD.
saqs.a: Xerostomia (candidiasis, halitosis, metallic taste), uraemic stomatitis, mucosal pallor, gingival overgrowth (cyclosporine/nifedipine), petechiae/bleeding, and loss of lamina dura/loose teeth (osteodystrophy).

saqs.q: State the timing and bleeding precautions for dental care in a dialysis patient.
saqs.a: Treat the day AFTER dialysis (avoid the dialysis day — heparin bleeding); never use the AV-fistula arm for BP/injection. Haemostasis with desmopressin (or cryoprecipitate).

saqs.q: Summarise the drug precautions in renal failure.
saqs.a: Avoid nephrotoxics — NSAIDs/aspirin; avoid tetracycline (use doxycycline); penicillin/metronidazole at lower dose; no systemic fluoride (topical OK); avoid magnesium antacids.

saqs.q: Outline the key points of renal transplantation relevant to dentistry.
saqs.a: More effective than dialysis; needs lifelong immunosuppression. Clear all dental infection beforehand; cyclosporine causes gingival swelling and is contraindicated with erythromycin; watch for infection/bleeding/hepatitis.
